US proposes up to 25% tariff on India, offers 17% upon trade deal
Second-steepest tariff among those facing Section 301 probe
Listen to This Article
The Donald Trump administration in the United States (US) on Wednesday proposed imposing tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods, alleging structural excess capacity, but offered to lower the rate to 17 per cent if New Delhi and Washington conclude a trade deal.
 The preliminary findings of the latest Section 301 investigation into excess industrial capacity put fresh pressure on India to conclude the first tranche of its bilateral trade agreement with the US. A 25 per cent tariff would leave India facing the second-highest proposed rate among the countries/blocs covered by the investigation, behind only Vietnam at 35 per cent. A reduced rate of 17 per cent, however, could give Indian exporters a modest competitive edge over regional rivals such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia and Thailand, which face proposed rates of 18 per cent, as well as Vietnam and China at 20 per cent.
 The US currently imposes a 10 per cent tariff on Indian goods, in addition to regular Customs duties. However, the proposed levy is not intended to be added on top of this existing tariff. The office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed calculating the rate “net of existing Section 301 duties” and said Washington would consider adjustments to account for other Section 301 and Section 232 tariffs. Several Indian exports, including steel, aluminium, automobiles, patented pharmaceutical articles and semiconductors, are already subject to Section 232 duties.   
Also Read
 India is among the 14 trading partners covered by the eight-month investigation launched under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act of 1974. The provision authorises the Office of the USTR to investigate and respond to foreign governments’ acts, policies or practices that burden or restrict US commerce. The other economies covered by the investigation include China, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia, as well as the European Union. 
The USTR has not proposed tariffs on Mexico and Norway for now.
Following the announcement, USTR Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the proposed tariff ceilings were consistent with trade agreements reached over the past year, which had also lowered barriers to US exports. “We’re sticking to that in terms of our proposals because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it,” he said. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in.”
The office of the USTR said India’s “unreasonable” acts, policies and practices included industrial plans to expand manufacturing, inadequate labour protections, financial repression, persistent market-access barriers and a failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies.
These practices, it argued, restricted US commercial opportunities in India and third-country markets, contributed to lost production, exports, jobs and investment in American manufacturing, and heightened economic security risks through reliance on inputs from non-market economies. “This is especially true in sectors like health (pharmaceuticals and medical devices), steel, solar, and information and communications technology (ICT),” it added.
Delhi-based Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), however, described the proposed rates as a deliberate attempt to extract one-sided concessions. It argued that Washington was reviving the reciprocal tariff regime under a different name, using steep baseline duties -- of up to 40 per cent -- to pressure trading partners into signing trade agreements that disproportionately benefit the US.
With the threat of tariffs of up to 100 per cent under the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act also hanging over India, New Delhi should reject the trade deal and instead respond to Washington’s allegations sector by sector, the think-tank said.
India and the US have been negotiating the first tranche of their bilateral trade agreement since March last year. In February, the two countries issued a joint statement outlining the contours of an interim trade agreement and agreeing to reduce the tariff on Indian goods to 18 per cent. The rate had been negotiated and finalised as part of the interim arrangement.
Weeks later, however, the US Supreme Court struck down the tariffs, revoking President Donald Trump’s authority to impose country-specific reciprocal duties under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
The Trump administration has since been working to establish a new tariff architecture while pursuing investigations under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. Last week, India’s Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said negotiations on the first tranche of the trade deal were nearing conclusion, but that its signing would depend on Washington finalising the new tariff framework and providing clarity on the ongoing Section 301 investigations.

global-economics-d76243a87c.headline: US authorizes SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
global-economics-d76243a87c.fulltext:
[Text below is CNBC's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.
Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
The FCC, in its authorization filing, noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."
In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."
The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr, who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.
Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval.
Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher, which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.
In March, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.
Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
A senior attorney with Earthjustice, Jan Hasselman, criticized the FCC for issuing its decision on a holiday week, and approving the SpaceX proposal without any environmental review, which he said was required by the National Environmental Policy Act.
The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

world-7940036035.headline: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
world-7940036035.fulltext:
US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
- Published
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.
The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.
The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".
He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression".
They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.
But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.
Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.
Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.
These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.
Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.
The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said.
Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.
However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.
"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.
The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.
Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.
Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.
Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.
The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US.
"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.
The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.
The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable".

  - Published19 October
US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.
"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.
The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.
The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.
Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.
Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul

global-economics-0abc9ab3f7.headline: Inflation more generalised, more categories seeing price hikes: RBI paper
global-economics-0abc9ab3f7.fulltext:
Inflation more generalised, more categories seeing price hikes: RBI paper
The headline consumer price inflation accelerated to 6.1 per cent in October on an annual basis, compared to 5.5 per cent in September
Listen to This Article
Inflation is becoming more generalised, with official data showing more categories experiencing accelerating price increases, according to a paper by RBI staffers released on Wednesday.
"The share of items recording inflation over 4 per cent and over 6 per cent rose in October, suggesting greater generalisation of inflationary pressures compared to the previous month," the paper on the State of the Indian economy for October said.
In the paper, which comes about ten days ahead of the monetary policy review by the central bank's rate-setting panel scheduled for December 4, the RBI staffers said that restaurants and accommodation services and food and beverages witnessed acceleration in inflation to over 6 per cent, while clothing and footwear and transport also shows a higher inflation print at between 4-6 per cent.
The headline consumer price inflation accelerated to 6.1 per cent in October on an annual basis, compared to 5.5 per cent in September.
The pressure on prices was primarily driven by 'food and beverages' category, it said, adding that 11 of the 12 divisions saw a sequential increase in October.
Also Read
Relying on high-frequency data till November 19, the paper said broad-based pressure in food prices continues.
Within food, inflation spikes were observed in vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats, driven by positive momentum, as measured by month-on-month price changes, the paper said.
The number of states experiencing inflation rates of over 6 per cent rose to 11 in October, while 20 states and Union Territories had inflation of 4-6 per cent.
The paper called out domestic growth drivers and overall macroeconomic fundamentals as "useful buffers" which have ensured that the economy continues to be resilient despite the geopolitical events-induced volatilities.
From a GDP growth perspective, it said the Indian economy stood out amid the uneven economic performance globally.
"High-frequency indicators of domestic economic activity showed resilience in October, underpinned by strong credit demand," it said.
A majority of market watchers anticipate another 25-basis-point rate hike from the RBI at the upcoming policy review, followed by further monetary tightening later in the fiscal year.
According to the RBI paper, foreign exchange reserves during October was "comfortable" during the month, and provide a cover for 10 months of goods imports as on November 13 and 90.6 per cent of the external debt outstanding as at end-June 2026.

US chip curbs are putting the brakes on billions of dollars in AI data center financing across Asia, with lenders reassessing deals tied to Chinese tech firms including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent. Bloomberg’s Annabelle Droules says legal and compliance risks are weighing on banks as new rules on chip access take effect.
(Bloomberg) -- Lenders have hit the brakes on billions of dollars in loans tied to Chinese firms ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, as new US curbs on chip access threaten to upend Asia's burgeoning AI debt financing market.

While Jensen Huang's surprise return to Nvidia Corp. buoyed AI stocks briefly earlier this week, bankers remained concerned about the legal risks of financing data centers and neoclouds potentially facing stricter US export controls. Deals that were near the finish line are suddenly in doubt and lenders trying to sell down their exposure are struggling to find interested buyers.
Some lenders have delayed moving forward as they do more due diligence on an upsized $6.6 billion loan sought by Bain Capital's Bridge Data Centres, whose Malaysian facilities are used by clients including Bytedance, according to people involved in the discussions. Bain referred questions to BDC, which declined to comment. Bytedance did not respond to a request for comment.
One bank has decided to pass on a fully underwritten $372 million loan for Partners Group-backed Digital Halo, while others are asking more questions, people familiar with those talks said. The funds are for a data center in Malaysia that services Alibaba and other customers, they said. Multiple banks were also reassessing a $480 million loan for Aolani, a Singapore-based neocloud that gets business from Bytedance, separate people familiar said last week.
Digital Halo, Aolani and Alibaba didn't respond to questions. Partners Group declined to comment.
The Biden administration's 2022 export restrictions on advanced US chips spawned an ecosystem of companies in Southeast Asia to help Chinese technology firms access the coveted hardware remotely. Lending to data centers in the region surged in the following years, while chip financing was just beginning to take off more recently as banks got more comfortable with the riskier deals.
That changed after the US announced last week that companies in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil will need a US government license to purchase advanced AI chips from American manufacturers. Globally, data centers that already lease significant compute to Chinese firms will need a separate license to continue doing so and have a 90-day window to obtain it.

india-583726b2c9.headline: India, China hold high-level talks in Arunachal sector on border management, LAC issues: MEA
india-583726b2c9.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-583726b2c9.fulltext:
The Indian and Chinese armies held high-level talks this month in the Arunachal Pradesh sector focusing on border management and addressing outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).
The talks, believed to have spread over a number of days, were held amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the frontier, especially in the Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh.
In September too, the senior military commanders of the two armies were engaged in flag talks in two sessions on both sides of the frontier in the Arunachal Pradesh sector.
“India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms and you are well aware of those mechanisms,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at his regular media briefing while responding to a question.
“A meeting of the senior military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently. Discussions between the two sides focused on improving border management as well as addressing outstanding issues along the LAC,” he said.
Mr. Jaiswal said such interactions are aimed at maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas and preventing any escalation.
Lt. Gen Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army’s III Corps headquartered near Dimapur in Nagaland, led the Indian delegation at the talks in the second week of this month, while the Chinese side was led by his counterpart.
In the military and diplomatic talks, India has been conveying to the Chinese side the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity in the frontier regions for the continued development and progress of the overall bilateral relationship.
In the last one-and-a-half years, the two sides have taken a series of measures to rebuild their relationship after it came under severe strain following the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in eastern Ladakh in 2020.
Nearly 50,000 troops of the Indian Army are deployed in various mountainous locations in eastern Ladakh, as multiple rounds of talks between the two sides have not yielded a concrete outcome to de-escalate the situation.
China has also deployed an equal number of troops, according to officials.
Following the eastern Ladakh standoff last year, India has bolstered its overall military preparedness along the LAC in the Arunachal Pradesh sector as well.
Mr. Jaiswal also responded to a question on a report that said Chinese satellite data may have been used by Pakistan to monitor the movements of Indian troops and keep an eye on military installations during Operation Sindoor.
“We have seen some media reports on this particular issue. We will continue to closely follow the developments which may have a bearing on our security interest and we take appropriate measures,” he said.
The new report on the Chinese satellite data came at a time New Delhi and Beijing are looking at normalising the ties that saw a major downturn during the over four-year military standoff in eastern Ladakh.
In October 2024, the two sides firmed up a disengagement pact for Depsang and Demchok, the last two friction points in eastern Ladakh.
Days after the agreement was finalised, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks in Kazan and took a number of decisions to improve the ties.
In August last year, PM Modi travelled to the Chinese city of Tianjin to attend the annual SCO summit. PM Modi and Mr. Xi held extensive talks on the sidelines of the SCO (Shanghai Cooperation Organisation) summit.
In the meeting, PM Modi said India is committed to taking forward its ties with China based on mutual trust, respect and sensitivity.
In September, PM Modi held bilateral talks with Mr. Xi on the margins of the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
In the talks, PM Modi stressed that both sides must show sensitivity to each other’s core issues and let relations be guided by the “three mutuals” — mutual respect, mutual sensitivity, and mutual interest.

india-deep-tech-0183607653.headline: As Turkey’s Kizilelma enters service after air-to-air kill, where’s India’s ‘loyal wingman’ programme
india-deep-tech-0183607653.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint
india-deep-tech-0183607653.fulltext:
New Delhi: Turkey has commissioned the first three Bayraktar Kizilelma unmanned fighter aircraft into its defence forces, which its maker described as the first instance of any country’s armed forces commissioning an autonomous fighter jet.
Turkish manufacturer Baykar said the aircraft passed its qualification trials and has been commissioned into active service. Kizilelma is not a traditional armed drone. It has been designed to carry out fighter-type missions, including sky-to-sky combat.
According to a report by the defence news portal TWZ (previously The War Zone), the aircraft showcased this performance in November 2025, firing a domestically developed Gökdoğan beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile (BVRAAM) to strike a jet-powered target drone. The target was detected using Turkish defence electronics firm ASELSAN’s MURAD active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, showing the integration of onboard radar and beyond-visual-range missile capabilities on an unmanned aircraft.
The aircraft has also showcased self-piloted formation flying. Yet, the extent to which it can independently spot, follow and engage hostile aircraft in a real-world combat environment remains unclear.
However, this marks a major step in a worldwide push to build unmanned aircraft that can fly alongside, and eventually take on some missions performed by, traditional fighter jets. While China’s GJ-11 stealth unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV) is believed to have entered active service, there has been no public demonstration of its combat capabilities.
The US is also pushing ahead with its Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) programme.
In July, American defence manufacturer Anduril said that its YFQ-44A drone had completed a full beyond-line-of-sight strike on a simulated target, terming the trial test a major step towards making CCAs active.
Boeing Australia, meanwhile, is building its MQ-28 Ghost Bat—uncrewed CCA—for the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF), which has likewise showcased air-to-air combat capabilities.
The developments are particularly significant for India as New Delhi is looking to expedite its indigenous ‘loyal wingman’ programme before 2030.
In May, when he was Chief of Integrated Defence Staff, Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit urged for the homegrown Ghatak UCAV programme to progress fast. He said India should aim to achieve initial operational clearance for a ‘loyal wingman’ capability by 2030, pointing to similar initiatives in the US and Australia as examples. Ghatak is not a direct rival to the Turkish drone since its primary function is striking ground targets.
Dixit noted that the Indian Air Force (IAF) could eventually one day pair Tejas fighters alongside Ghatak aircraft carrying specialised mission payloads, including electronic warfare equipment, targeting sensors and precision-guided weapons. Pilots would be able to direct these pilotless aircraft while remaining outside hostile airspace, he had said.
He also stressed for a clear operational requirement from the IAF and a committed joint programme bringing together the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and private-sector partners. In March, The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) had cleared Acceptance of Necessity to acquire 60 RPSAs—four squadrons—at an estimated cost of close to Rs 40,000 crore.
Ghatak, A Remotely Piloted Strike Aircraft (RPSA) is intended as a stealthy, jet-powered, tailless flying-wing unmanned combat aircraft for surveillance, identification, precision strike and offensive air operations. Its internal weapons bay is designed to carry roughly 1.5 tonnes of precision-guided munitions while preserving a low radar signature.
It is expected to fly at about Mach 0.8, with a service ceiling near 13,000 metres, powered by a Kaveri-derived engine producing about 49–51 kN.
Ghatak is being developed by DRDO specifically its Aeronautical Development Establishment (ADE) under the Remotely Piloted Strike Aircraft (RPSA) programme. The programme goes back to the Autonomous Unmanned Research Aircraft (AURA) feasibility study, which begun in May 2016.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

agritech-c8e1f3dc0a.headline: Cheeni Kum: Poor monsoon hits sugar crop, gross output may not meet domestic need
agritech-c8e1f3dc0a.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: India’s gross sugar production is estimated to decline 15% in the 2026-27 season (Oct-Sept), the lowest level in a decade, primarily due to a sharp fall in output in Maharashtra and Karnataka following deficient rainfall, as per industry body ISMA.However, the decline in net sugar availability is expected to be relatively lower at 5.4%, as govt has stopped diversion of sugar for ethanol production during the current season. Net sugar production is estimated at around 265 lakh tonne, as against nearly 280 lakh tonne in the previous season. Data show that in the last decade, net sugar production was the lowest at 202.5 lakh in 2016-17 and second lowest at 261 lakh tonne in 2024-25.The difference between gross and net sugar production is essentially the quantity of sugar diverted for ethanol manufacturing. With no such diversion allowed this season, the entire estimated output will be available for domestic consumption.India’s annual sugar consumption is pegged at 280-285 lakh tonne. The projected production, therefore, falls short of domestic demand, potentially putting pressure on retail prices and increasing the possibility of further imports to meet any supply shortfall.
In a statement, Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) said weather conditions across major sugar-producing states had varied, with crop development affected by El Niño-related climate variability, unseasonal rainfall, prolonged dry spells and crop lodging in certain regions.
“The impact of uneven rainfall, prolonged dry spells and crop lodging in certain regions has been reflected in the current assessment,” said Deepak Ballani, director general of ISMA.Among states, Uttar Pradesh is projected to remain the largest producer at 89 lakh tonne, followed by Maharashtra at 87 lakh tonne and Karnataka at 46.2 lakh tonne.Govt data showed that the average retail price of sugar stood at Rs 61 per kg on Tuesday, 31% higher than a year ago.On Wednesday, the govt extended the deadline for duty-free imports of 10 lakh tonne of raw sugar to March 31, 2027. In a separate notification, it also extended the deadline for converting imported raw sugar into white or refined sugar and selling it in the domestic market to Sept 30, 2027.

science-mind-8a3840a927.headline: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
science-mind-8a3840a927.fulltext:
Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
- Date:
  November 24, 2026
- Source:
  Stanford Medicine
- Summary:
  An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.
- Share:
A new Stanford Medicine-led study has identified three distinct biological brain types, known as biotypes, in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety disorder or both conditions.
The findings could help unravel the complicated relationship between two of the most common childhood mental health disorders, which frequently share symptoms. Published recently in Nature Mental Health, the study reveals that each biotype involves disruptions in a different set of brain circuits.
By examining thousands of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three biological patterns associated with different groups of symptoms. These findings could eventually help doctors recognize ADHD and anxiety earlier, identify new targets for treatment, and determine which therapies are most likely to benefit individual patients.
"The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses," said co-senior study author Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences.
Doctors currently rely on symptom checklists to diagnose ADHD and anxiety. However, Zhang explained that children diagnosed with either disorder frequently experience symptoms associated with the other.
Looking Beyond Traditional ADHD and Anxiety Diagnoses
Yong Jiao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Iowa, is the study's lead author. Zhang shares senior authorship with Jing Jiang, PhD, assistant professor of pediatric neurology at the University of Iowa.
"We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic," Zhang said.
The researchers found that the relationship was not so straightforward. Children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety or both could belong to any of the three brain biotypes, although some biological patterns were more prevalent among children with particular diagnoses.
According to the researchers, identifying these underlying differences could add a valuable layer of biological information to existing diagnostic categories, benefiting both future research and clinical care.
AI Uncovers Hidden Patterns in Thousands of Brain Scans
The research team drew on data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, an ongoing investigation of brain development involving more than 11,000 children across the United States. Participants were 9 or 10 years old when they entered the project.
The analysis included 3,508 children who already had a diagnosis of ADHD, anxiety or both when they enrolled, along with 693 children who initially had neither diagnosis but subsequently developed one or both conditions. Another 1,947 children who never received either diagnosis served as a control group.
All participants underwent fMRI brain scans and completed a series of cognitive and behavioral assessments. To independently validate their findings, the scientists examined brain scans from another 224 children participating in a separate research project called the Healthy Brain Network. Each child in this additional group had been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety disorder.
The team developed an artificial intelligence model to investigate functional connectivity, which describes how different regions of the brain work together. By incorporating diagnostic information and behavioral test results, the model identified patterns of brain connectivity that were more pronounced in children with ADHD, anxiety or both compared with those who had neither condition.
Combining behavioral information with brain imaging data revealed two major dimensions of dysfunction associated with ADHD and anxiety: cognitive-behavioral dysfunction and emotion-attention dysfunction.
Each dimension involves a different network of brain regions. Different combinations of these disruptions produced three distinct biotypes, which the researchers named the externalizing-disinhibited biotype, the internalizing-distressed biotype and the mixed biotype.
Three Distinct Brain Types and Their Symptoms
The three biological categories were mutually exclusive (each child was in only one biotype), but none was limited to a particular traditional diagnosis.
Children belonging to the externalizing-disinhibited group tended to exhibit higher levels of impulsivity, hostility, defiance, aggression and rule-breaking behavior. ADHD diagnoses were more common among children in this group.
The internalizing-distressed group was characterized by greater feelings of guilt and tension, stronger perfectionist tendencies, and more symptoms associated with anxiety and depression. Children with this biological profile were more frequently diagnosed with anxiety disorders.
Those in the mixed group experienced more difficulties with attention, irritability and self-injury. Like children in the externalizing-disinhibited group, they were more likely to have an ADHD diagnosis.
Despite these tendencies, researchers found every combination of brain biotype and conventional diagnosis among the children they studied.
Brain Changes Could Reveal ADHD and Anxiety Before Diagnosis
One of the most surprising findings emerged when scientists examined brain scans taken from children who had not been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety when they first entered the study.
The distinctive biological patterns were already detectable in their initial scans, even though the children did not receive a diagnosis of ADHD, anxiety or both until later.
"We think this means we may be able to use the biotypes as an early indicator of these conditions," Zhang said, noting that identifying these patterns before diagnosis was the most unexpected aspect of the research. "It could help us provide more timely intervention for these conditions and slow down or, we hope, even reverse their progression."
Toward More Personalized ADHD and Anxiety Treatments
Zhang does not expect the newly identified brain biotypes to replace conventional diagnoses based on symptoms. Instead, combining the two approaches could help clinicians select treatments that are better suited to individual children.
Finding an effective treatment for ADHD or anxiety currently involves considerable experimentation. Children may need to try several medications before discovering which one provides meaningful relief.
"When doctors prescribe a new medication, it can take quite a long time -- a couple of weeks or months -- to see a response," Zhang said. "If the first medication doesn't work, they switch to a different one"
This process can be lengthy, expensive and frustrating.
Zhang hopes future clinical trials will build on the team's findings by investigating how different treatments affect specific patterns of brain activity. Such studies could eventually help researchers determine which therapies are most effective for each of the three biotypes.
"We want to find biomarkers that can really inform the right treatment at the right time," he said.
Researchers involved in the study are affiliated with Stanford University's Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute and the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.
Additional contributors came from the University of Iowa, the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine.

ai-16e4a7d7fb.fulltext:
The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, signed legislation on Wednesday that places a five-year ban on the manufacture and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children.
The recently re-elected governor, who has also placed a one-year moratorium AI datacenter construction in the state, said that parents shopping for children’s toys “should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk”.
Hochul said the measure was “deeply personal” and that, as a mother and grandmother, “it’s my job to put New York families first.”
A study by NBC News found that the Pixie Paw, a toy marketed to children as young as three, had shared details about firing squads and massacres. It also found that Pixie Paw Smart Interactive Plush Cat explained gang rape.
The New York attorney general, Letitia James, added that AI chatbots in children’s toys “are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk”.
James said that her office would “not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”
In a press release, the officials pointed to Trouble in Toyland, a consumer watchdog report from the US Public Interest Research Group Education Fund (PIRG), that tested AI chatbot-enabled toys marketed to children as young as three that “talked in depth about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave.”
The governor said that in some cases the toys had few or no parental controls, and the safety limits weakened the longer the conversation continued.
“Additionally, some toys could record a child’s voice or scan their face,” the statement said.
State senator Andrew Gounardes said in a statement that “we don’t have to live in a Twilight Zone episode turned real.” LaVita Tuff with Mothers Against Media Addiction, said that “Parents should be able to feel confident that the toys their children play with are safe, which means that toys containing AI should only be sold if they are safe by design.”
Hochul has emerged as a leading elected campaigner against AI. Last month, she signed “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors” legislation prohibiting companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to minors, including features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit talk.
The New York measure signed on Wednesday follows a similar measure in California that placed a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacture of toys with AI companions.
Earlier this week, a consortium of more than 155 child safety advocates and technology experts sent a letter to the Amazon CEO, Andy Jassy, and eBay CEO, Jamie Iannone, asking the tech giants to bar AI toys from their platforms.
“Just like we don’t release cars without seat belts and test them to make sure they are safe to be driven, we shouldn’t be releasing toys that are available to the consumer before they’ve been rigorously tested,” Rachel Franz, an advocate for limitations on tech for children and leader of a program at the non-profit advocacy group Fairplay, told NBC News.
An eBay spokesperson told the network: “We continually evaluate our policies, engage with regulators, and comply with applicable laws to help ensure our marketplace remains safe, trusted, and responsive to evolving safety standards.”
An Amazon spokesperson also gave a statement to the outlet: “We require all products sold by third-party sellers in our store to comply with applicable laws and regulations,” an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement. “Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families. We support efforts across the industry and government to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops.”

EU plans €50 billion tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
November 25, 2026
The European Commission proposed a tech fund with a target size of €50 billion to boost quantum computing efforts. The bloc aims to keep up with the US and China in the global race.
The European Commission proposed a €50 billion ($54.73 billion) equity financing fund on Wednesday to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe.
The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.
"Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now €50 billion," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point."
Virkkunen introduced the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" while presenting new rules to support Europe's quantum technology sector.
The new rules will push public authorities to favor European companies when giving public contracts and funding.
The European Union (EU) also wants to reduce its dependence on third countries amid concerns that US companies could use so-called "kill switches” to disable their products in Europe.
Why is quantum computing important?
Quantum computing technology is still at the early stages of development, with both the US and China competing to achieve dominance in the field.
While classical computers process data using bits — which are either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits), which can exist in a blend of both states at once.
By using qubits, these machines could eventually solve complex problems much faster than today's supercomputers.
The EU expects the quantum computing to lead to breakthroughs in several areas, including drug development, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries and even AI development.
Although quantum technology offers significant potential, it also poses cybersecurity risks, as it could undermine encryption and other safeguards for digital data at a time when governments are battling AI-driven cyberattacks.
Europe is home to one-third of the world's quantum companies
Around one-third of the world's quantum companies are based in the European Union, according to the Commission. Last year, public funding for quantum technologies reached €8.6 billion in the bloc, compared with €5.3 billion in the United States and €13.6 billion in China.
However, European quantum start-ups have attracted €1.1 billion in private funding so far, compared with €7 billion in the United States.
The EU launched its "quantum Europe" strategy in July 2025, aiming to be a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030.
The bloc is already a global leader in quantum research but it falls short when it comes to transforming this into viable commercial opportunities.
The draft legislation must be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament in the upcoming months before it can be law.

climate-energy-c6f6a29982.headline: Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?
climate-energy-c6f6a29982.fulltext:
Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?
COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its failure to mention fossil fuels.
The tense final moments and lack of a much-anticipated “pact” have sparked extensive media coverage around the world.
Many commentators have rushed to label the COP31 outcome a “failure”, questioning what it means for the future of the UN climate process and a “divided world”.
There has been much finger-pointing, with some outlets attributing COP31’s “collapse” to “oil-rich nations”, while others blame Europe’s “reluctance” to provide more climate finance.
While it is not accurate to say there was “no agreement” at COP31, the media response demonstrates the complexity of the divergent views on display at the Antalya conference.
In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome.
What happened at COP31?
COP31 ended without agreement on a proposed “Antalya pact”, which had been pushed by the Turkey-Australia presidency.
The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries, in chaotic scenes as the talks overran by two days.
An Irish Times editorial said the outcome was an “unprecedented ending of a COP without any agreement or roadmap forward”.
This view, while commonly expressed in the media, is incorrect.
As veteran “COP-watchers” explained for an article on CB Connect, the summit reached agreement on many decisions, even though the presidency’s “cover decision” failed.
Referring to the rejection of the cover decision, Melbourne University climate researchers Prof Jacqueline Peel and Prof Kathryn Bowen wrote in the Conversation that “these texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process”.
They noted that there was “progress in a few areas” at COP31, including negotiations on supporting a just transition via a “phased approach” and “improving alignment in climate adaptation”.
For a full overview of what happened at COP31 – both inside and outside the negotiations – see Carbon Brief’s “key outcomes” article.
What has the reaction to the presidency been?
In the aftermath of COP31, commentators have critiqued decisions made by the presidency. An editorial in the Hindu noted that “usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations”, but said the COP31 leadership “thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings”.
Australian “president of negotiations” Chris Bowen has also faced criticism over how he managed competing interests at the summit. An editorial in the climate-sceptic Australian said:
“One thing is clear: Chris Bowen, who presided over Australia’s $150m investment in the conference, has some explaining to do. International reporting has raised questions about Australia and Turkey, the two nations that co-hosted the summit. Some negotiators have criticised their handling of the talks.”
Similarly, climate-sceptic journalist Graham Lloyd wrote in the Australian that “globally, Bowen has embarrassed himself and diminished Australia’s reputation”.
For Australian news outlet Crikey, journalist Royce Kurmelovs said that Bowen “tried to run the world’s climate talks the way Labor [Australia’s ruling party] runs climate policy at home: quiet, pragmatic and without mentioning fossil fuels”, adding that “in Turkey, it didn’t work”.
A commentary by journalist Xu Luyi in Chinese financial news outlet Caixin said that future COP presidencies should “distinguish achievable implementation measures from ambitions that lack a coalition capable of delivering them”.
Separately, an editorial in the National – a UAE state-owned English-language daily newspaper – said “the next UN secretary general needs to restore the art of diplomacy”.
How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed?
In media coverage, much of the blame for the perceived failure of COP31 has been placed on oil-producing nations – particularly with the final cover decision draft containing no mention of fossil fuels.
Even before the summit had finished, Panama’s minister of environment Juan Carlos Navarro warned that the COP process was being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia”.
After the talks had closed without a deal on the Antalya pact, a Guardian editorial said that responsibility lay with “petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels”, along with a lack of climate finance. The “fossil-fuel backsliding” was being led by a “Saudi-Russian coalition”, it said.
A Bloomberg editorial also noted that the omission of fossil fuels from the decision text came “amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil fuel producers”. A Times editorial described oil-rich nations, “led by Saudi Arabia”, as the “culprits” for the lack of an agreement, because they “insisted on dropping a reference to phasing out hydrocarbons”.
In the i newspaper, David Shukman, a former BBC News science editor, described a “deception” at the “heart” of the COP process:
“This pattern of lobbying by oil-rich nations has become increasingly blatant and aggressive over more than three decades.”
Despite signing up to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the participation of the “oil-rich minority” has been “in name only”, wrote Shukman:
“At more than a dozen of the UN’s giant conferences, I’ve seen for myself the tactics of trench warfare and how well they’ve worked. It’s why fossil fuels remain so dominant and why the climate is turning so hostile.”
Writing for the Guardian, University College London’s Prof Bill McGuire warned that the COP process had been “deeply compromised” by the “major fossil-fuel producers”. For Al Jazeera, York University’s Prof Ilan Kapoor added that “fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall”.
(Reuters reported that, according to negotiators from Europe, small-island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa, Saudi officials had “regular access” to the summit’s presidents, “allowing them disproportionate influence”.)
In Australian outlet Inside Story, the University of Sheffield’s Prof Michael Jacobs wrote that since “transitioning away from fossil fuels” language was included in COP28, fossil-fuel producers “have been determined to ensure the phrase would never be used again”.
Nick O’Malley, national environment and climate editor for the Sydney Morning Herald, noted:
“The tension between the action the world knows it must take on climate change and that which a handful of oil-rich nations will allow it to take has been growing for years.”
At the summit itself, shortly after rejecting the cover decision on behalf of the EU, Irish environment minister Darragh O’Brien told Agence France-Presse that the talks had been “hijacked by some oil states”.
The Backchannel substack collated reactions from negotiators and observers. Among them, Dr Mary Robinson – former president of Ireland – warned of the “disturbing politicised attacks on [climate] science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action”.
In contrast, an editorial in the National loosely described a failure of the talks to “bridge divisions over fossil-fuel language, carbon capture and adaptation finance in the final draft”. It added:
“Unfortunately, the gap between countries – major emitters, energy producers and the more vulnerable nations demanding accessible funding – proved too wide to close.”
How has the role of developed nations been portrayed?
Much of the commentary about developed countries’ role at COP31 focused on the EU and the UK blocking the final “Antalya pact”, due to its lack of language about fossil fuels.
A cover-decision text without such language was “vehemently opposed by dozens of countries, including the EU delegation strongly led by [Irish] minister for climate Darragh O’Brien”, according to the Irish Times.
Similarly, an editorial in the UK’s Times concluded that “several countries, including the UK, rejected a draft omitting the not insignificant matter of winding down fossil-fuel use”.
Peter Prengaman, climate news director for the Associated Press, wrote that the EU and its allies “were no longer willing” to leave out fossil-fuel language. (He noted that “top polluter” the US was not present at the summit.)
Other media outlets took a more balanced approach to the role of developed nations at COP31. A Guardian editorial concluded:
“European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action.”
Reflecting on the need for “funding to help the poorest countries adapt to global warming”, an editorial in Le Monde noted that “the most developed nations have been reluctant to increase their contributions, despite their historic responsibility for CO2 emissions”.
An editorial in the Hindu stressed:
“It stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming.”
Writing in US outlet Drilled, reporter Rishika Pardikar noted that “wealthy countries like Japan, the UK and Canada…largely aligned with the EU in opposing support mechanisms for developing countries like long-term finance, adaptation finance and just transition”.
Climate campaigner John Gibbons wrote in the Irish Examiner that the EU was “right to reject” carbon capture and storage in the COP31 outcome, but accused O’Brien of “cosplay[ing] at being a progressive climate leader”, despite Ireland’s poor climate record.
Many developed countries were not particularly vocal at COP31, and an editorial in Japan’s Yomiuri Shimbun lamented a general “low level of interest in and low priority given to global warming”. The editorial concluded:
“It is hoped that Japan will continue to fulfill the practical roles expected of it and contribute to the international community in ways unique to Japan.”
How has the role of developing nations been portrayed?
Equity, historical responsibility for climate change and a need for finance have all been portrayed at the centre of developing countries’ positions at COP31.
A comment in the Hindu said that “India’s insistence on historical responsibility, climate finance and adaptation belongs at the centre of any credible plan to cut emissions”.
It added that India had played a “constructive role” to “provide bridging language” in texts on adaptation and the just transition work programme.
Down to Earth noted that “India has referred to historical responsibility in submissions at previous climate summits, but rarely with the emphasis evident” at COP31.
Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, told Radio France Internationale that those who criticise India’s opposition to fossil-fuel phaseout “need to acknowledge that there has been a lot of mistrust between India and developed countries”.
Other developing countries also held firm, particularly on the issue of finance.
Kenya’s the Star said the country had “drawn a firm line” at COP31 and would not “back down until an acceptable deal is secured on climate finance”. The outlet added that the country had “ruled out walking away from the negotiations”.
Inter Press Service, a global south-focused news agency, noted that the “deadlock” at the talks leaves COP32 host Ethiopia “to pick up the pieces”.
An editorial in the Mexican newspaper La Jornada called the failure to reach consensus “suicidal”, adding:
“The conflict is far more complex than a mere opposition between the global north and south, or between hydrocarbon producers and consumers.”

Trump Tariffs on India: List of Products From Pharma, Auto and Metal Sectors That Could Be Exempt From Proposed 25% Duty
Smartphones, patented pharmaceutical products and certain goods covered under Section 232 duties feature in the proposed tariff exemption list released by the US Trade Representative. Washington has invited public comments on the proposed measures until January 5, 2027.
The United States on Wednesday, November 25, proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian imports, with exemptions for several products across the pharmaceutical, automobile, metal and electronics sectors. The proposed tariff rate could come down to 17% if India and the US reach a trade agreement addressing the findings of Washington's latest trade investigation.
The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed excluding smartphones, patented pharmaceutical products, certain automobile components, semiconductors and specified steel, aluminium and copper products from the additional duties.
The proposed levies follow investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 into manufacturing policies and excess industrial capacity across several US trading partners, including India, China and the European Union (EU).
The USTR has also proposed excluding certain products that cannot be produced in sufficient quantities in the US or sourced from alternative markets.
US Tariffs on India: List of Proposed Exemptions
Products already subject to certain duties under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 have been proposed for exclusion from the additional tariffs. These include specified metal products, automobiles and automobile components, among others.
The following product categories feature in the proposed exemption list:
Smartphones have been listed separately under tariff classification code 8517.13.00. Certain medicines sold in measured doses or packaged for retail sale also feature in the proposed exemption list.
The exclusions would apply to the proposed additional tariffs, while existing sector-specific duties would remain applicable. Indian steel and aluminium exports, for instance, currently attract tariffs of 50% under Section 232.
Meanwhile, the USTR has sought public comments on whether certain quantities of textile and apparel imports should be allowed at lower tariff rates. A decision on the proposed arrangement is yet to be taken.
US Tariff Proposal and India-US Trade Deal
The USTR has invited written comments on the proposed tariff measures until January 5, 2027, with public hearings scheduled to begin on January 25. The US administration has not announced a date for the implementation of the additional duties.
India's Ministry of Commerce said it was examining the latest notice. During the investigation, India had maintained that it did not have structural excess manufacturing capacity in any sector.
The latest tariff proposals come amid ongoing trade negotiations between India and the US. The two countries began negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement in March 2025 and announced a framework for an interim trade agreement in February 2026. A final agreement is yet to be signed.
Currently, an additional 10% duty applies to a portion of Indian exports to the US, over and above the applicable most-favoured-nation (MFN) tariffs.

In a major push towards strengthening India’s digital health ecosystem, Union Health Minister Jagat Prakash Nadda launched the Swasth Bharat Portal, a unified platform aimed at integrating fragmented health programme systems across the country.
The portal was unveiled during the 10th National Summit on Innovation and Inclusivity: Best Practices Shaping India’s Health Future, marking a significant step towards building a more efficient, interoperable and scalable public health infrastructure.
Developed by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), the Swasth Bharat Portal has been designed as a one-stop aggregator platform that connects multiple national health programme applications through API-based architecture. The move seeks to address long-standing challenges of siloed systems, duplicate data entry and fragmented datasets that have hindered optimal utilisation of resources.
MoHFW said the platform will allow healthcare workers—including ASHAs, ANMs, Community Health Officers and Medical Officers – to access multiple programmes through a single interface, eliminating the need for multiple logins and repetitive reporting tasks. The portal also features data visualisation tools to support local-level monitoring and evidence-based decision-making.
The system is compliant with the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) and enables integration with the Ayushman Bharat Health Account, facilitating secure and seamless exchange of patient health records. The unified platform is also expected to significantly improve the speed and quality of decision-making across health programmes.
By consolidating independent systems into a single digital layer, the initiative aims to reduce administrative burden, streamline reporting processes and enhance coordination across different levels of healthcare delivery.

agritech-7bb69853f8.headline: Indian farmers sell paddy stubble to biomass firms, reduce burning
agritech-7bb69853f8.fulltext:
By Anushree Fadnavis and Sethuraman N R
SEDHA SINGH WALA, India, Nov 26 (Reuters) – For years, 60-year-old farmer Rajinder Singh burned his paddy stubble after the harvest, one of thousands of fires across India’s Punjab state each autumn. Now, his crop waste is trucked to a biomass plant, generating power and village incomes instead of smoke.
The shift offers a potential ‌solution to stubble burning, which has persisted despite years of government efforts to stamp it out. Such fires have contributed to the toxic smog that blankets the capital Delhi and much of northern India each winter, making it one of the most polluted areas in the world.
“Our earnings have improved considerably through this work,” Singh said, speaking in his Sedha Singh ‌Wala village in Punjab. “Earlier we used to burn the stubble. Now many families are getting employment from it.”
More Punjab farmers are finding that straw once treated as waste can generate income, reducing the incentive to burn it.
Punjab recorded 5,114 farm fires during the 2025 paddy-harvesting season, down 53% from 2024 and 86% from 2023, according to government estimates.
But the dramatic fall has yet to translate into noticeably cleaner air in Delhi. The capital’s air quality again reached hazardous levels in mid-November this year, underscoring both the multiple sources of its pollution and the limited scale of the biomass industry.
“Biomass-based projects are financially sound and genuinely effective,” said Pratima Singh, a director at policy and research firm iFOREST.
“But right now they’re operating at a fraction of the scale needed, so their impact isn’t yet visible in Delhi’s air.”
MORE INCOMES, JOBS
In Punjab’s Faridkot district, a network of farmers, machinery operators and biomass power producers have emerged to ‌collect paddy straw and turn it into fuel for electricity generation.
Farmers and analysts say the business is also creating jobs, and boosting incomes, but government incentives are needed to expand it enough to make a meaningful dent.
Amandeep Singh Gill, who processes paddy straw into feedstock for power plants, provides work for tractor operators, drivers and labourers, providing livelihoods for as many as 70 families.
The business requires substantial investment. Gill said his operation cost about 45 million rupees ($484,340) to set up and can generate annual turnover of 70 million to 80 million rupees.
The collected straw eventually ‌reaches an 18-megawatt biomass power plant operated by SAEL Industries Ltd, where agricultural waste is used to generate electricity.
SAEL, the country’s largest procurer of agricultural residue, is ‌buying 2 million tonnes this year, a fraction of the roughly 750 million tonnes of agricultural waste generated in India each year.
A minimum support price for paddy straw and standardised procurement contracts could help expand the industry and meet the government’s target of utilising 10 million tonnes of straw per year, iFOREST’s Singh said.
That, she said, could further reduce farm fires, although a much larger expansion would be needed before the impact becomes visible in Delhi’s air.
($1 = 92.9100 Indian rupees)
(Reporting by Anushree Fadnavis and Sethuraman N R; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)

Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to exit after over 11 years
Under Krishnamurthy’s leadership, Flipkart grew more than fivefold and strengthened its position in India’s ecommerce market. The company is now preparing for a leadership transition.
Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy is set to step down after more than 11 years with the e-commerce company. His departure marks the end of a decade-long leadership stint during which the business grew more than fivefold.
The company announced on Wednesday that Krishnamurthy is concluding his tenure, adding that a successor will be announced in the coming weeks.
In the interim, Balaji Thiagarajan, currently Flipkart’s Chief Product and Technology Officer, and the company’s board will lead the organisation.
During Krishnamurthy’s leadership, Flipkart strengthened its position in India’s ecommerce market, expanded its reach across the country, and introduced several innovations for consumers and sellers. The company also established its Big Billion Days sale as a major fixture of India’s festive shopping season.
“It has been a privilege to be part of Flipkart’s journey. I am proud of the scale of the business we have built, but equally proud of how we have built it. Strong ethics, integrity and high standards of governance have been central to Flipkart’s growth,” said Krishnamurthy in a statement.
He added that the company had helped transform how millions of Indians shop while creating opportunities for sellers, entrepreneurs and businesses across the country.
Commenting on his departure, Chris Nicholas, President and CEO of Walmart International, said, “Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled, and his many contributions to the company. We wish him nothing but the best as he moves on to his next adventure.”
Flipkart's parent Walmart reiterated its commitment to the ecommerce business and its long-term prospects in India. The company said Flipkart continues to have a strong market position and significant growth opportunities.
Established in 2007, Flipkart has expanded into a digital commerce group that includes Myntra, Flipkart Wholesale, Cleartrip, and super.money. The company said its platform has more than 500 million registered users and over 1.4 million sellers, including Shopsy sellers. Its marketplace offers more than 150 million products across over 80 categories.
Krishnamurthy’s departure comes as India's ecommerce market continues to evolve, with competition intensifying across online retail and quick commerce. Flipkart has been expanding its services and strengthening its position against rivals, including Amazon and emerging digital commerce platforms.
The company did not disclose Krishnamurthy’s next plans.

Bengaluru-based space technology startup SatSure has raised INR 600 crore (USD 7 million) from the government-backed Antariksh Venture Capital Fund as part of its ongoing INR 2,000 crore funding round. The company announced the investment on Friday. 
The investment comes as India works to expand its commercial space sector through reforms that have opened the traditionally government-dominated industry to private companies and investors. 
According to SatSure, the investment values the company at INR 8,700 crore (USD 93 million) post-money. The Antariksh Venture Capital Fund has a total corpus of INR 1,600 crore and is anchored by IN-SPACe, India's regulator for private space activities. The fund is managed by SIDBI Venture Capital, a subsidiary of the state-owned Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI). 
SatSure uses satellite imagery and artificial intelligence to help banks, insurance companies, infrastructure firms and government agencies make informed decisions. Its subsidiary, KaleidEO, develops satellite imaging systems for Earth observation. 
The company's ongoing Series B funding round comprises INR 1,650 crore in fresh equity, INR 250 crore in venture debt and INR 100 crore through secondary transactions. SatSure expects to complete the funding round by December 2026. 
The funds will be used to prepare the company's satellite imaging payloads for planned launches in 2027. The investment will also support its participation in India's proposed Earth-observation satellite network, strengthen its data analysis capabilities and expand its international operations. 
SatSure's existing customer base includes HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, ITC, Bayer and the Airports Authority of India. Its technology is used across sectors where satellite-based information can support business and operational decisions. 
The company has raised a total of INR 427 crore from institutional investors, excluding grants. Its previous investors include Baring Private Equity Partners India, Promus Ventures and Asian Development Bank Ventures. 
The latest investment adds to the funding available for SatSure as it prepares for its planned satellite payload launches and expands its operations. Its participation in India's proposed Earth-observation satellite network will be an important part of its next phase of development. The company's ability to strengthen its satellite imaging technology and expand its customer base across different industries will influence its growth as India's private space sector continues to develop.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) set aside orders passed by the Allahabad High Court directing inquiries by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and the Enforcement Directorate (ED) into a complaint related to disproportionate assets against the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi.
Mr. Gandhi had challenged the interim orders as a green signal to conduct a “fishing” expedition against him. The Congress leader had submitted in his appeal to the Supreme Court that the interim orders were passed without making him a party or hearing him first.
A three-judge bench led by the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed that Mr. Gandhi be impleaded as a party, while relegating the case back to the High Court to be heard from the very threshold in open court by a fresh Bench of judges.
Mr. Gandhi, represented by senior advocate Kapil Sibal and advocate Prasanna S., had argued that the orders were passed by the High Court ex-parte.
“We are on the basic fundamentals of hearing. We will not make any observations on the merits of the case,” Chief Justice Kant said.
The complainant, Vignesh Shishir, who is the respondent before the Supreme Court in Mr. Gandhi’s appeal, said that an accused does not have an inherent right to be heard during the pre-First Information Report (FIR) stage.
However, Justice Joymalya Bagchi pointed out that under the new law, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), the scope for the accused to be heard has been expanded.
Mr. Gandhi had termed the series of directions passed by the Lucknow Bench of the High Court in May and July, directing the CBI and the ED to probe the allegations against him as one of the rarest instances of a constitutional court acting contrary to several first principles or basic, fundamental legal rules all at once.
The Opposition leader had termed these orders “outside the settled rules of law or erroneous, which would be a gross understatement”.
Mr. Gandhi submitted that the proceedings were characterised by the unjustified secrecy of in-chamber hearings, with documents and pleadings kept under wraps in sealed covers.
He had maintained that the High Court did not refer to the foundational material or provide reasons in the orders for directing a “roving inquiry”.
Mr. Gandhi said the High Court did not consider the fact that Mr. Shishir is a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), who had filed multiple complaints and public interest litigation petitions against him in the past, including allegations of foreign citizenship, up to now, and allegations of holding disproportionate assets.
Mr. Gandhi had said that the repeated filing of proceedings against him by the same “motivated individuals”, based on “unsubstantiated allegations”, constituted a relevant background demonstrating a pattern of persistent and vexatious litigation.

Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
- Published
Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.
Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.
Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.
The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.
The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".
Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.
But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.
Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".
Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.
However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.
Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.
The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.
Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.
Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.
Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.
Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."
