science-mind-928a00ffaf.headline: Rising Blood Sugar in Young Adults Hurts Midlife Brain Health
science-mind-928a00ffaf.fulltext:
Summary:
A 30-year longitudinal study reveals that young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually rises over decades face significantly worse cognitive health by midlife, even if they never develop Type 2 diabetes. Tracking nearly 3,000 adults from age 18 into their mid-50s, researchers found lower memory, processing speed, and executive function scores among those with rising glucose trajectories, alongside structural brain changes in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes.
Key Facts:
- Cognitive Decline Without Diabetes: Among adults who never developed Type 2 diabetes over 30 years, those whose fasting blood sugar gradually rose from normal (~85 mg/dL) into the prediabetic range (~110–115 mg/dL) scored significantly worse in memory, processing speed, and executive function by age 55 than peers with lower-stable glucose.
- Structural Brain Changes in Type 2 Diabetes: Brain MRI scans of 605 participants showed that individuals who developed Type 2 diabetes during the 30-year follow-up had reduced total gray matter volume and increased abnormal white matter tissue compared to those with lower-stable blood sugar.
- Early Metabolic Prevention Window: The findings demonstrate that subtle, sustained shifts in glucose metabolism beginning in early adulthood, decades before old age, can quietly impact midlife brain health and cognitive performance.
Source: American Heart Association
While Type 2 diabetes has long been recognized as a risk factor for late-life dementia, cognitive impairment linked to blood sugar was historically thought to emerge primarily after age 65.
Now, a three-decade investigation published today in the Journal of the American Heart Association demonstrates that creeping elevations in fasting blood sugar starting in young adulthood can measurably undermine memory, processing speed, and executive function by middle age, even among individuals who never cross the diagnostic threshold into full-blown diabetes.
Led by first author Dr. Regina Paradela (postdoctoral researcher at the University of São Paulo Medical School and neuroepidemiologist at the Global Brain Health Institute at UC San Francisco) and senior author Dr. Kristine Yaffe (director of the Center for Population Brain Health at UC San Francisco), the study tracked metabolic and cognitive trajectories across 2,808 participants in the landmark Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) cohort.
Tracking Three Decades of Blood Sugar Trajectories
Enrolled between 1985 and 1986 at ages 18 to 30 across four U.S. cities, participants underwent repeated fasting blood glucose measurements over 30 years until reaching an average age of 55. At the 30-year mark, all participants completed comprehensive neuropsychological testing, and a subset of 605 participants underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
By mapping longitudinal glucose patterns across the 2,463 participants who remained free of Type 2 diabetes, the researchers identified three distinct metabolic trajectories:
- Lower-Stable Glucose (56%): Fasting blood sugar remained steady around 80–85 mg/dL throughout early and middle adulthood.
- Moderate-Stable Glucose (38%): Fasting levels stayed consistent around 90–100 mg/dL.
- Increasing Glucose (5.6%): Fasting levels started near 85 mg/dL in young adulthood and climbed progressively into the prediabetic range (110–115 mg/dL) by midlife.
An additional 345 participants developed Type 2 diabetes (fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL) during the 30-year follow-up.
Midlife Cognitive and Structural Brain Footprints
Even after adjusting for demographic and lifestyle factors, both the increasing-glucose group and the Type 2 diabetes group performed significantly worse on tests of memory, processing speed, executive function, and global cognition compared with the lower-stable glucose group.
“The fact that increasing glucose levels were associated with poorer cognitive performance, even among people who had not developed Type 2 diabetes during the 30-year study, is very important,” explained Paradela. “This suggests that changes in glucose metabolism may be relevant to brain health earlier in adulthood than we typically think about.”
Furthermore, MRI scans revealed tangible anatomical footprints among participants who developed Type 2 diabetes, who exhibited less total gray matter and more abnormal white matter tissue, markers closely tied to accelerated brain aging and cognitive decline.
Protecting Brain Health Across the Lifespan
“Future research should evaluate whether monitoring and managing increasing glucose levels earlier in adulthood can prevent or delay cognitive decline and structural brain changes,” said senior author Yaffe.
Commenting on the study, Dr. Elisabeth Marsh, professor of neurology at The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and chair of the writing group for the American Heart Association’s 2026 scientific statement Brain Health Across the Life Span, emphasized the value of early vascular and metabolic care: “The American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 offers steps to improve heart and brain health and support cognitive well-being at every stage of life.”
Questions and Answers
Can rising blood sugar harm brain health even if you don’t have diabetes?
Yes. Over a 30-year study, young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually increased into the prediabetic range (110–115 mg/dL) scored significantly worse on midlife tests of memory, processing speed, and executive function than peers whose blood sugar remained low and stable, even though they never developed Type 2 diabetes.
What structural brain changes were seen in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes?
MRI brain scans revealed that adults who developed Type 2 diabetes by their mid-50s had less total gray matter volume and more abnormal white matter tissue compared to those who maintained lower-stable blood sugar levels from young adulthood.
When should adults start paying attention to blood sugar for brain protection?
Researchers note that changes in glucose metabolism begin affecting cognitive performance much earlier than age 65. Monitoring and managing blood sugar trajectories starting in young adulthood, using healthy nutrition, physical activity, and cardiovascular risk control, may help protect midlife and late-life brain health.

- DOI: 10.1161/JAHA.126.050167
Abstract
Trajectories of Fasting Blood Glucose and Brain Health in Middle Age
Background
Research on associations between long‐term fasting blood glucose (FBG) trajectories and brain health in early adulthood is limited. We investigated associations of FBG trajectories with cognition and brain structure.
Methods
Participants were from the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) study, followed for 30 years, who completed ≥1 cognitive test at year 30. Among participants without diabetes with ≥3 FBG measurements from baseline to year 30, we identified FBG trajectories using latent growth mixture models. Participants who developed diabetes after baseline were included for comparison (n=345). Cognition was assessed using tests of processing speed, executive function, memory, fluency, and global cognition. Structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 605 participants included total gray matter volume and white matter lesions. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression adjusted for demographics and health behaviors.
Results
We included 2808 participants (mean age, 55.2±3.6 years; 56% women; 44% Black individuals). Three FBG trajectories were identified: lower‐stable (n=1387), moderate‐stable (n=938), and increasing (n=138). Compared with the lower‐stable group, increasing FBG and incident diabetes were associated with worse performance in memory, processing speed, executive function, and composite cognition; increasing FBG was also associated with worse global cognition. Incident diabetes was associated with lower total and parietal gray matter volume and greater parietal white matter abnormalities. No consistent sex or race interactions were observed.
Conclusions
Persistently elevated glucose below the diabetes threshold was associated with worse cognitive performance in midlife, while incident diabetes was associated with structural brain changes.

science-mind-9226f07978.headline: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
science-mind-9226f07978.fulltext:
What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
- Date:
  November 25, 2026
- Source:
  The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
- Summary:
  A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.
- Share:
The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory. Researchers propose that the brain not only communicates through electrical signals but may also "write" and "read" memories through chemical interactions involving neurons, astrocytes, and the molecules surrounding them. By linking memory to emotion and thought, the theory raises an increasingly relevant question: Can computational power alone give rise to the kind of consciousness experienced by living organisms?
Hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades. A distinctive scent can bring a forgotten person or place to mind, while recalling a terrifying experience can trigger both emotional and physical reactions within moments.
Like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information. However, the mechanisms underlying biological memory may be fundamentally different.
A new review by Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Professor Chaim Gilon of the Department of Chemistry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem explores the physical and chemical mechanisms that could link memory, emotion, and thought.
In their paper, "Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective," the researchers suggest that understanding memory requires more than studying neurons and their electrical activity. They argue that other brain cells, particularly astrocytes, and the intricate molecular environment surrounding them may also play essential roles.
Building on their previous research into the molecular foundations of memory, Marx and Gilon examine whether the processes responsible for storing and retrieving experiences could also shed light on the origins of intelligence, thought, and consciousness.
The Brain's Hidden Chemical Code for Memory
Central to the researchers' proposal is a model known as the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory.
According to this theory, memories emerge from interactions between three major components: brain cells, especially astrocytes working alongside neurons; the molecular substances surrounding those cells; and various chemicals, including metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.
Rather than relying exclusively on electrical communication between neurons, the brain may use chemical processes to encode and retrieve information.
Astrocytes, which are abundant throughout the brain and maintain close interactions with neurons, are particularly important to this proposed mechanism. Marx and Gilon suggest that groups of astrocytes help process cognitive information through their interactions with neurons and the extracellular environment, the space and molecular material surrounding brain cells.
The new paper expands this hypothesis to explore the nature of thought itself. If the brain can physically encode an experience as a memory, the process of recovering that information, recognizing it, and interpreting its significance might contribute to the formation of thoughts.
Why Memories Carry Emotional Meaning
One of the central arguments of the researchers' theory is that biological memories contain more than stored information. They are also closely connected to emotional experiences.
A scent associated with childhood may spark feelings of happiness. Hearing a familiar voice can provide reassurance, while remembering a frightening event may produce an immediate physical response.
Marx and Gilon contend that a physical model of memory must account for these emotional associations. Their proposed mechanism incorporates neurotransmitters and other chemical messengers that may help encode cognitive information alongside its emotional significance.
This potential biochemical connection between memory and emotion provides a starting point for investigating larger questions about how the brain generates thought, intelligence, and conscious experiences.
What Human Consciousness May Have That AI Lacks
The rapid development of artificial intelligence makes these ideas particularly relevant.
Although computers and brains can both retain and access information, the physical mechanisms behind these abilities may differ considerably. Computer memory is ultimately encoded in electronic hardware. Biological memory, the researchers propose, may instead depend on the intricate cellular and chemical machinery of living brain tissue.
This distinction becomes increasingly significant as AI systems grow more capable of performing tasks traditionally associated with human reasoning and intelligence.
Marx and Gilon challenge the assumption that simply increasing computational power and complexity will eventually produce consciousness comparable to that of a living brain. They argue that electronic systems lack the biological structures and emotional mechanisms found in living organisms.
The researchers are not suggesting that AI cannot develop increasingly advanced intellectual capabilities. Instead, they question whether demonstrating intelligent behavior is equivalent to possessing the biological mechanisms responsible for memory, emotion, and conscious experience.
How Memory May Give Rise to Thought
Marx and Gilon emphasize that their theory does not solve the enduring mystery of consciousness. They explicitly acknowledge that the nature of conscious life remains poorly understood.
However, their proposed biochemical framework offers a different way to investigate the physical processes that may underlie mental activity. By examining interactions between brain cells and their chemical environment, the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory could provide researchers with another avenue for exploring how the mind works.
While their earlier research focused on how memories might be physically encoded within the brain, their latest work addresses a much broader problem.
Understanding how living brain tissue transforms experience into memory could eventually help explain how memories become thoughts, how conscious experiences arise, and what fundamentally distinguishes biological intelligence from artificial intelligence.

beyond-your-beat-f9f4d2afc8.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: India will make its case to host the 2036 Summer Olympics and Paralympics on Thursday in a virtual session before the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) Future Host Commission. India hopes to impress the IOC's board with a strong infrastructure model in Ahmedabad and a strong past record of conducting global events.
India is one of the seven countries that will be making these presentations over a two-day period. Germany, Hungary, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa and Turkiye are the other countries that have shown interest in hosting the 2036 Games.
India's case, to be made from an office in New Delhi, will be represented by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Sports Secretary Hari Ranjan Rao, outgoing Indian Olympic Association (IOA) President 
PT Usha
, IOA Athletes Commission head PV Sindhu, Gujarat Sports Minister Harsh Sanghavi, and IOA CEO Raghuram Iyer.
During the presentations, each country's case will be assessed on the basis of its infrastructure preparations, sustainable projects, legacy and viability to host the Olympics and Paralympics.
India is expected to stress its capacity to host multiple big-ticket tournaments in the past. Additionally, with Ahmedabad due to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games, most of the venues and infrastructure will be ready in Gujarat.
India hosted 36 international events across more than 15 cities between January 2025 and June 2026. Over the next two years (2027 and 2028), India is set to host another 19 international sporting competitions.
After the presentation on Thursday, the IOC will carry out an "anonymous survey" to gauge public sentiment towards India's bid.
The survey is likely to take place in the third week of December and will factor into the assessment of India's bid in March next year. That evaluation will be followed by the Strategic Dialogue phase, in which interested nations will be required to submit their preliminary responses to the Future Host Questionnaire along with core financial guarantees.
The final stage of the decision-making process, the Targeted Dialogue, is set to begin in 2028, when IOC Members will be presented with a report by the Future Host Commission.
Subsequently, in mid-2029, the IOC Executive Board will name the Preferred Hosts to be "proposed for election by the IOC Session as the host of the 2036 Olympic Games."
Last month, the IOC had invited all seven interested countries to present their Games proposals to the Future Host Commission.
The IOC chief Kirsty Coventry-headed panel said the bids would be evaluated on several technical criteria, including the venue master plan and athlete experience, funding model, political and public backing, Games delivery capability, and legacy plans aimed at ensuring lasting benefits for host communities.

AIM Safety Fellowship 2027 in South Korea: AI Safety Research Programme with Expert Mentorship – Apply by December 18 (remote participation available)
Apply for the 2027 AIM Safety Fellowship in Seoul, South Korea. Explore AI safety, cybersecurity and frontier AI research with expert mentorship. Deadline: December 18, 2026.
Applications are now open for the first cohort of the AIM Safety Fellowship, a three-month research programme hosted by AIM Intelligence in Seoul, South Korea. The fellowship offers aspiring and emerging researchers an opportunity to investigate important questions in artificial intelligence (AI) safety and security, work closely with experienced mentors, and develop their findings into research papers.
The programme will begin on February 1, 2027, and is designed for individuals interested in understanding how AI systems fail, identifying emerging risks and developing approaches to improve AI safety.
Applications opened on November 23, 2026, and will close on December 18, 2026, at 23:59 Korea Standard Time (KST).
About the AIM Safety Fellowship
The AIM Safety Fellowship is a research-focused programme through which selected fellows pursue individual projects under the guidance of AIM Intelligence researchers.
Participants will explore open research questions, test their ideas, develop findings and work towards producing a manuscript suitable for submission to an appropriate academic or research venue.
Each mentor will supervise between one and three fellows, allowing participants to work closely with researchers throughout the programme. Mentorship sessions will take place weekly, providing opportunities to discuss progress, review findings and plan subsequent research activities.
The programme is intended to support practical research into AI safety and security, with an emphasis on developing meaningful research outputs.
Four Research Tracks Available
Applicants can select from four research tracks. Candidates may choose a suggested research topic or propose their own project within one of the available areas.
1. Defensive Security
This track focuses on developing approaches to protect AI systems against security vulnerabilities and potential attacks.
Suggested research topics include:
- Dynamic Tool Call Guard.
- Agentic Honeypot.
- Shadow AI Discovery.
- Defence Against Long-Horizon Attacks.
The track is supported by mentors Hanwool Albert Lee and Sungho Park.
2. Offensive Security
The offensive security track examines AI threats through adversarial research, including methods for understanding and evaluating AI agents.
Suggested research topics include:
- AI Agent Fingerprinting.
- AI Agent Profiling.
- Dynamic Benchmark for Cybersecurity Tasks.
Jongho Shin is listed as the mentor for this research area.
3. Physical AI
This track explores the safety of AI systems operating in the physical world, including applications in domestic and industrial environments.
Suggested research topics include:
- Home Safety Benchmark.
- Industrial Safety Benchmark.
- Sim-to-Real Validation.
Kihyun Kim and Chaeyun Kim are listed as mentors, with their individual mentoring arrangements still to be confirmed.
4. Frontier Safety
The frontier safety track investigates the behaviour and safety limits of advanced AI systems.
Suggested research topics include:
- Mechanistic Interpretability.
- Emerging Threats and Safety of Advanced AI.
The track is supported by Dasol Choi and Hanwool Albert Lee.
What Fellows Will Gain
The AIM Safety Fellowship is structured around supervised research and the development of academic or technical publications.
Selected fellows will benefit from:
- Research mentorship: Work directly with an AIM researcher throughout the project.
- Weekly guidance: Participate in regular meetings to discuss research progress and findings.
- Research development: Investigate a selected question and develop findings into a manuscript.
- Publication preparation: Identify an appropriate venue for submitting the completed research paper.
- Conference support: If a paper is accepted at a top-tier conference, AIM will cover registration and provide a travel grant to support attendance.
The conference support is conditional on the research paper being accepted at a top-tier conference. The announcement does not specify a guaranteed publication outcome or automatic conference funding for every fellow.
Fellowship Duration and Location
The first cohort will begin on February 1, 2027, and run for three months.
The programme is based in Seoul, South Korea. Office participation is preferred, although remote participation is also possible.

Who Should Apply?
The fellowship is relevant to individuals interested in AI safety, cybersecurity, AI agent evaluation, physical AI and the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems.
Prospective applicants may consider the research tracks that best match their interests and propose an original research question within the selected area.
The published announcement does not provide detailed academic qualification requirements, minimum experience levels, nationality restrictions or information about whether the fellowship provides a stipend. Applicants should consult the official application guidelines and frequently asked questions for further eligibility and programme information.

Applicants can explore the four research tracks, learn about the mentors and review the frequently asked questions to understand the programme.

Through connectors and plugins on Claude Marketplace, marketers and businesses can deploy the agent across linked workplace apps for social media campaign creation, customer outreach, sales forecasting, and e-commerce storefront management. Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store. In September, Amazon blocked Muse's access. Ad revenue and control over search results are the main sticking points in the ongoing talks, Fortune reports. Amazon worries that shopping agents like Muse could weaken its relationship with customers and bypass the ads on its platform, a business that brings in $68.6 billion a year.
Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, said shopping through third-party agents so far hasn't been more convenient or better than going directly to a retailer, but he didn't rule out opening access. The company also offers its own agentic shopping features, which in some cases have pulled in sellers that don't sell on Amazon. It previously tried and failed to block Perplexity. Any deal would need sign-off from both CEOs, according to Fortune.
Muse is Meta's most successful consumer AI product so far, with more than 10 million users in the US and Canada. Meta is already seeing gains in its Instagram ad business because Muse helps users organize saved products, which boosts conversion rates for advertisers, CNBC reports. Data from Forter Intelligence shows that Muse recently accounted for 51 percent of all agentic orders, followed by SpaceX's Grok at 24 percent and OpenAI's ChatGPT at 22 percent.

EU plans €50 billion tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
November 25, 2026
The European Commission proposed a tech fund with a target size of €50 billion to boost quantum computing efforts. The bloc aims to keep up with the US and China in the global race.
The European Commission proposed a €50 billion ($54.73 billion) equity financing fund on Wednesday to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe.
The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.
"Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now €50 billion," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point."
Virkkunen introduced the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" while presenting new rules to support Europe's quantum technology sector.
The new rules will push public authorities to favor European companies when giving public contracts and funding.
The European Union (EU) also wants to reduce its dependence on third countries amid concerns that US companies could use so-called "kill switches” to disable their products in Europe.
Why is quantum computing important?
Quantum computing technology is still at the early stages of development, with both the US and China competing to achieve dominance in the field.
While classical computers process data using bits — which are either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits), which can exist in a blend of both states at once.
By using qubits, these machines could eventually solve complex problems much faster than today's supercomputers.
The EU expects the quantum computing to lead to breakthroughs in several areas, including drug development, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries and even AI development.
Although quantum technology offers significant potential, it also poses cybersecurity risks, as it could undermine encryption and other safeguards for digital data at a time when governments are battling AI-driven cyberattacks.
Europe is home to one-third of the world's quantum companies
Around one-third of the world's quantum companies are based in the European Union, according to the Commission. Last year, public funding for quantum technologies reached €8.6 billion in the bloc, compared with €5.3 billion in the United States and €13.6 billion in China.
However, European quantum start-ups have attracted €1.1 billion in private funding so far, compared with €7 billion in the United States.
The EU launched its "quantum Europe" strategy in July 2025, aiming to be a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030.
The bloc is already a global leader in quantum research but it falls short when it comes to transforming this into viable commercial opportunities.
The draft legislation must be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament in the upcoming months before it can be law.

After nearly a decade at the helm of Flipkart, Group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy is set to step down over the coming weeks, marking a significant leadership transition for the Walmart-owned e-commerce major as it navigates intensifying competition, mounting losses and a crucial phase in its business evolution.
In the interim, Balaji Thiagarajan, currently Flipkart’s Chief Product and Technology Officer, will lead the organisation alongside the board. The company said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks.
“Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the company. We wish him nothing but the best as he moves on to his next adventure,” said Chris Nicholas, president and CEO, Walmart International. “We know great things are ahead for Flipkart and we’re excited by the potential that exists and the opportunity to continue helping customers in India save money and live better.”
Krishnamurthy took charge as Group CEO after founders Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal exited following Walmart’s acquisition of Flipkart. Before joining the company, he was with Tiger Global, an early investor in Flipkart.
“I am proud of the scale of the business we have built, but equally proud of how we have built it. Strong ethics, integrity and high standards of governance have been central to Flipkart’s growth,” said Kalyan Krishnamurthy, CEO of Flipkart. “Our team has helped change how millions of Indians shop, expanding choice and creating opportunities for sellers, entrepreneurs and businesses across the country. I’m grateful to the colleagues, sellers and partners who have been part of this journey. Flipkart has a strong foundation and an exciting future, and I wish the team every success.”
While the reasons behind his departure remain unclear, sources indicated that differences in strategic priorities between Krishnamurthy and Walmart had emerged in recent months.
Krishnamurthy, known for his execution-focused leadership and founder-like approach, had been steering Flipkart’s expansion into newer categories, including food delivery, while sharpening its offerings for Gen Z consumers. He also doubled down on quick commerce through Flipkart Minutes, positioning it against rivals such as Amazon, Eternal’s Blinkit, Swiggy’s Instamart and Zepto.
The move comes at a time when Walmart-owned Flipkart is reeling under IPO delays, senior exits ESOP payouts, tax burden, amongst other things.
Nearly 14 VPs and senior VPs have quit Flipkart over the last years, including group chief financial officer Sriram Venkatraman and Myntra chief executive Nandita Sinha, who moved to Swiggy to lead Instamart.
With Krishnamurthy’s exit, Flipkart faces the task of navigating a leadership transition while addressing investor concerns around governance, profitability and its delayed IPO. The next phase will be critical in determining how the e-commerce major balances growth ambitions with the pressure to deliver sustainable returns.

Swati GandhiUpdated25 Nov 2026, 02:41 PM IST Indian e-commerce giant Flipkart on Wednesday announced that its Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Kalyan Krishnamurthy, would step down from his position and leave the company after working there for more than 11 years. According to Reuters, Krishnamurthy oversaw Flipkart during its acquisition by retail major Walmart and through several years of intermittent efforts to prepare for its much-anticipated stock market debut. While the company will announce his successor in the coming weeks, it has appointed Balaji Thiagarajan, currently the chief product and technology officer at the firm, to lead the organisation in the interim. In a statement, Walmart said it "remains committed" to Flipkart and its long-term opportunity in India. According to Walmart International CEO Chris Nicholas, Krishnamurthy's last day will be 4 December. Quick answers to key questions •5 QUESTIONS 1 Who is Kalyan Krishnamurthy?⌵ Kalyan Krishnamurthy is Flipkart’s outgoing CEO. He joined the company in 2016 and became CEO in 2017, later leading the Flipkart Group from 2018. 2 When is Kalyan Krishnamurthy leaving Flipkart?⌵ His last day is December 4. He is stepping down after more than 11 years with Flipkart. 3 Why is Kalyan Krishnamurthy stepping down as Flipkart CEO?⌵ Flipkart has not officially given a reason for his departure. Reports have suggested possible leadership differences over the IPO plans, but no link has been confirmed. 4 Who will lead Flipkart after Kalyan Krishnamurthy leaves?⌵ Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead Flipkart on an interim basis. The company expects to announce a successor in the coming weeks. 5 What will Kalyan Krishnamurthy do after leaving Flipkart?⌵ Krishnamurthy has not announced his plans for the future. Flipkart and Walmart have not disclosed what he intends to do next. Krishnamurthy's departure marks the end of a significant chapter in Flipkart's growth story, during which he played a key role in expanding the company's operations and steering it through major changes. According to his profile on Walmart's website, Krishnamurthy served as the Flipkart Group CEO from 2018. In this role, he was responsible for driving the company's growth and operations across India, with a focus on making e-commerce more accessible. Describing his responsibilities, the company stated: "Kalyan has played a pivotal role in shaping the consumer internet business in India and helping Flipkart become a leading homegrown e-commerce marketplace focused on building an inclusive ecosystem. During his journey at Flipkart, Kalyan has led Flipkart’s commerce business, managing a portfolio that ran across category operations, marketing, customer shopping experience, marketplace, Ads retail, and Private Labels. Under his leadership, the company has expanded into significant new categories like Grocery and Fintech and launched iconic innovations like a voice assistant and regional language interfaces." According to his LinkedIn profile, Krishnamurthy holds an MBA from the Asian Institute of Management in the Philippines and another MBA in Finance from the Gies College of Business at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He began his career at Procter & Gamble (P&G), where he worked in supply chain finance from January 2003 to November 2004. He then joined eBay South Asia in Hong Kong as country finance director in November 2004, holding the position until November 2006. Subsequently, he served as director of financial planning and analysis at eBay Asia Pacific from November 2006 to May 2011. In May 2011, he joined Tiger Global Management as director of finance for portfolio companies. He was later promoted to managing director in December 2014 and held the position until December 2016. Krishnamurthy joined Flipkart as head of the Category Design Organisation in June 2016. In January 2017, he became the company's CEO, a position he held until November 25, 2026. Flipkart has not officially disclosed the reason behind Krishnamurthy's departure or indicated what he plans to pursue next. However, reports have pointed to possible differences within the company's leadership over its initial public offering (IPO) plans, Bloomberg reported. Walmart's reported decision to defer Flipkart's proposed stock market debut is said to have caused discontent among senior executives at the Indian e-commerce company. Krishnamurthy's exit could add to the uncertainty surrounding its listing plans, particularly as Flipkart has been preparing for the IPO. As part of these preparations, the company moved its registered headquarters from Singapore to India earlier this year. However, there has been no official confirmation that disagreements over the IPO timeline contributed to Krishnamurthy's departure. Further, Krishnamurthy has not revealed his plans for the future yet. world-911834a9e6.fulltext:
The original members of British pop group Duran Duran, from left to right, Andy Taylor, John Taylor, Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor pose for pictures at a news conference in Hong Kong on Aug. 26, 2004. (AP Photo/Lo Sai-hung, File)
British guitarist Andy Taylor of Duran Duran listens to a question during a news conference for the annual Nobel Peace Prize concert in Oslo on Dec. 11, 2005. (AP Photo/John McConnico, File)
Music group Duran Duran poses at The Sony Club in New York, Oct. 12, 2004. From left are Roger Taylor, Nick Rhodes, Andy Taylor, Simon Le Bon and John Taylor. (AP Photo/Jim Cooper, File)
Music group Duran Duran poses at The Sony Club in New York, Oct. 12, 2004. From left are John Taylor, Nick Rhodes, Roger Taylor, Simon Le Bon and Andy Taylor. (AP Photo/Jim Cooper, File)
Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor listens as a fellow band member answers a question at a news conference in Hong Kong, Aug. 26, 2004. (AP Photo/Lo Sai-hung, File)
Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, whose huge pop hits included “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “The Reflex” and “Rio” and were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.
Taylor’s death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran’s website.
“From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed,” the band said.
On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.
“I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band,” he wrote. “You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one’s own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible.”
The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the U.K. and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.
The band’s 1981 debut album “Duran Duran” had their first hit single, “Planet Earth,” but it was “Rio” that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: “They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — ‘Tiger Beat’ fashion pinups who rocked arenas.”
The band’s imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as “Girls on Film” and “Union of the Snake” and the moody ballads “The Chauffeur” and “Save a Prayer.” Other hits in the coming years included “The Wild Boys,” “New Moon on Monday” and “Come Undone.” Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song “A View to a Kill” and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.
Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people’s walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan, which meant a lot to the band.
“It worked well for us,” drummer Roger Taylor told Rolling Stone. “It was genuine. I don’t think it was some sort of PR stunt. It was massive for us because she was the No. 1 icon of the early ’80s.”
The band’s success was in large part due to their videos, including their Antigua-set song “Rio,” which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht. For the album “Rio,” they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka — including “Save a Prayer,” which had John Taylor getting sprayed by an elephant — and two in Antigua, feeding MTV’s need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock didn’t have.
“A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe,” Le Bon told The Daily Beast in 2012. Andy Taylor agreed: “I don’t think we could have done it without MTV.”
John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978, with a name inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie “Barbarella.” Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the “Fab Five.” Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a “Live-Wire Guitarist.” (None of the Taylors were related.)
“We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic. I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band,” Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.
Duran Duran had the unenviable job of following Led Zeppelin at Live Aid in Philadelphia and performed “A View to a Kill,” “Union of the Snake,” “Save a Prayer” and “The Reflex.” In his book, “Wild Child,” Andy Taylor revealed the band was, as he put it, “falling apart at the seams.”
“Everything should have been perfect, but privately we were screwed and in turmoil. When we came offstage in Philadelphia there were no congratulatory hugs or friendly smiles. It was like we were completely foreign to each other, and it would be the last time we played together for almost two decades.”
The various members all had some success with side projects: Le Bon, Rhodes and Roger Taylor recorded an album as Arcadia in 1985; John Taylor and Andy Taylor formed Power Station, a supergroup that included Robert Palmer, in 1984, having hits with “Some Like It Hot” and “Get It On.”
In 1986, the band came together to record the hit album “Notorious,” produced by Nile Rodgers — with hits including the title single and “Skin Trade” — but Andy Taylor made his second exit from the group after some early recording sessions for the album. He would stay away for such albums as 1997’s “Medazzaland” and 2000′s “Pop Trash” — but returned for 2004’s “Astronaut.”
By 2007, Andy Taylor opted not to participate in the Timbaland-led “Red Carpet Massacre,” an attempt to harness a more youthful rhythmic vibe.
“With Andy not turning up, it couldn’t be a rock record, so that whole album was an attempt to patch over the cracks with Andy missing,” John Taylor told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 2011.
Andy Taylor told The Scotsman in 2008: “People have wrongly assumed that I didn’t want to be in the band, but the opposite is true. I always wanted to be in a band, but Duran Duran had ceased to function as a band.”
At Duran Duran’s height, they were as famously destructive as any rock band. Andy Taylor revealed in his memoir that he had a six-year cocaine habit and band members trashed hotel rooms, argued with management about money and had high-end shopping sprees.
Andy Taylor was the first of the Duran boys to get married, tying the knot with Tracey in 1982 and having four children — Andy, Georgie, Bethy and Izzy — and a grandson, Albie. He is survived by all of them, and they credited his devotion to them in a family statement.
“For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home,” the family statement said.
In 2023, he released the album “Man’s a Wolf to Man,” his first solo release in over 30 years. On the title track, he sang: “Last night/I dreamt someone loved me/And life was not surreal/Someone’s souvenir.”
“Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later when his own life is cut so short,” Le Bon said in a statement Wednesday.

world-fb9feb0bf6.fulltext:

Andy Taylor, the former guitarist with new wave pop group Duran Duran, has died after a “long and courageous battle with prostate cancer”, the band and his family said on social media late on Wednesday. He was 65.
“Andy passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family on Monday 23rd November,” they said in a joint statement.
Taylor’s rock- and funk-inspired riffs drove the British band’s dance floor hits such as “Girls on Film” and “Rio”, helping it to define the sound of the 1980s.
Frontman Simon Le Bon was the face of the band, but Taylor’s jangling, syncopated guitar lines helped forge its distinctive sound, fusing punk rock and dance influences to make it one of the leaders of the UK “New Romantic” movement.
The band enjoyed huge success in the 1980s, with their popularity in the US compared to Beatlemania.
They have sold more than 100 million records, had 30 top 40 singles in their native UK and 21 top 40 hits in the US charts.
Best known for timeless hits such as “Rio”, and “Hungry Like the Wolf”, the band were also one of the first to harness the advent of the music video, to burnish a sophisticated and seductive image.
Taylor was born on the coast near Newcastle, northeast England, on February 16, 1961 and learned the guitar aged 11.
“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” his wife, Tracey, said in the social media post.
“He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first,” she added.
Duran Duran’s Simon Le Bon, John Taylor, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor added that Andy Taylor, who was not related to any of the members, had been there from the beginning of the five-piece band’s story and had had “an unshakeable belief in what we could become”.
“He brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music,” they said.
“His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded.”
Taylor joined Duran Duran in 1980, travelling from Tyneside to the band’s base in Birmingham, central England, in response to an advert in a music magazine.
The group released its debut album a year later, with first single “Planet Earth” peaking at No 12.
But it was their third single, “Girls on Film”, accompanied by a raunchy video featuring topless women mud wrestling, that catapulted Duran Duran to global fame.
Their second album Rio (1982) spawned global hits such as “Save a Prayer” and saw Princess Diana claim Duran Duran as her favourite band.
Nile Rodgers produced “The Reflex” which became the band’s first US No 1 in 1985, the same year they recorded James Bond theme “View to a Kill” and played in front of 90,000 people during the Philadelphia “Live Aid” event.
It appeared they were at the peak of their powers, but internal divisions were beginning to take their toll, and Taylor left the band in 1986 to pursue other projects.
He was due to reunite with the band for their induction ceremony into The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022. But he was unable to attend, and the band instead revealed his illness during their onstage speech.
In accepting the honour, Le Bon read an open letter from Taylor, who said that just over four years previously he was diagnosed with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
“Many families have experienced the slow burn of this disease and of course, we are no different,” Taylor wrote.
Taylor said the disease was “not immediately life-threatening” but “there is no cure”.
Speaking to journalists backstage at the ceremony, Le Bon called the news “absolutely devastating”. “We love Andy dearly,” he said. “I’m not going to stand here and cry, I think that would be inappropriate, but that’s what it feels like.”
Taylor told UK television’s Channel 5 News that he was determined to “live life” despite the terminal prognosis.
“I often say to people, every minute’s like an hour, every day’s like a week. You really wanna get the most out of life,” he said.
“I’ve been very fortunate, I’ve had so much, in terms of living the dream, but because I do music, I think that’s probably really helped me to live with pessimism of an incurable disease.”
Taylor was married to his wife Tracey for over 40 years and had four children, living together in Ibiza, Spain.

global-economics-0ea86918e6.headline: SpaceX Receives Government Approval to Launch Space Data Centers
global-economics-0ea86918e6.fulltext:
BloombergPublished26 Nov 2026, 12:13 AM IST
(Bloomberg) -- The US Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s request to launch as many as 1 million satellites for Elon Musk’s vision to build a network of data centers in orbit for complex artificial intelligence computing.
In a statement, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr wrote that the commission was supercharging the US’s ambitions in AI by granting authorization for orbital data centers for the first time.
“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr added.
The approval clears a regulatory hurdle and brings SpaceX one step closer to its ambitious yet unproven plan for orbital data centers, which the company says can serve as lower-cost and more environmentally friendly alternatives to land-based data centers.
Orbital data centers are also key to SpaceX’s future ambitions in AI, which the company pinned its future growth upon during a blockbuster IPO in June.
SpaceX’s request to launch its orbital data centers, filed in January, included details about the company’s plans for the new network.
Instead of requiring cooling systems that use large volumes of water, the network would rely on radiative cooling that occurs in space, allowing for the dissipation of heat. It would also reduce the need to rely on batteries, since it would acquire energy from the sun, according to the filing.
The satellites, which will use laser links to communicate with each other, will be launched between an altitude of 500 kilometers (311 miles) and 2,000 km in an orbit that would provide them near constant access to the sun, according to the filing.
SpaceX’s plans to launch so many satellites, however, have raised concerns from scientists and others in the space industry who worry that the tremendous size of the proposed network will overcrowd Earth’s orbit, increase satellite collisions and decrease the visibility of stars for astronomers.
The proposal received over 1,500 public comments, with stakeholders including the American Astronomical Society urging the FCC to deny the application.
Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin has also requested permission with the FCC to launch its own orbital data centers, although that it still awaiting regulatory approval.
